title: Lowbrow/"Poor" films enjoyed by high profile critics/directors

commenti.body:
I know this is the opposite of your question format, but I think it’s sort of relevant and totally hilarious…. I saw John Waters live the other week and he spent a decent amount of time talking about his favourite filmmakers (all very highbrow, unsurprisingly) and particularly Pasolini.  I’m sure we can all guess what his favourite Pasolini film was.

All this to say, I believe people who have the best grasp of art appreciate both the high and low brow.  So I love your question because it can be pretty informative as to a person’s tastes - oh, you make art?  Tell me about your favourite trash!

Tarantino has plenty that fit this criteria, but one of his most notable is his love of Unstoppable, the schlocky thriller with Chris Pine and Denzel about a train that won’t slow down. There’s a decent Rewatchables pod about it. 

And not sure how “lowbrow” it is but I know Kubrick was a very big fan of White Men Can’t Jump.

Alfred Hitchcock loved Smokey and the Bandit

Hitchcock was primarily seen as just an entertainer and low brow for a while until the Cahiers crowd - primarily Truffaut - continued their high praise, with the latter mentioned director famously interviewing him and then having the conversations put to text and released as Hitchcock/Truffaut. 

I’m sure Hitchcock appreciated the quick-witted dialogue between the characters, the adventure and fun atmosphere of the film.
Seeing Waters live must've been a delight! And with your avatar I can tell you're clearly a fine art critic Mr Gablogian

Kubrick liked White Men Can't Jump? Outstanding, these gems are what I'm here for. 

Also I think Unstoppable is one of those generic sounding films done many times that on a technical level is very well done (could probably go for most Tony Scott films). Tarantino's enthusiasm for all film is so infectious.

Yeah, a list of his favorites was [compiled for Criterion](https://www.indiewire.com/news/general-news/stanley-kubricks-favorite-films-included-the-jerk-white-men-cant-jump-modern-romance-101486/):

>Over at Criterion, Joshua Warren has compiled a list of Stanley Kubrick’s favorite films, a list he gathered from interviews with friends, family, and colleagues as well as from an interview Kubrick did about fifty years ago. While there are certainly a fair amount of high-brow titles on the list, you may be surprised to learn just how… diverse it is.The list Warren compiled includes titles from the Criterion Collection, such as “Henry V,” “I vitelloni,” “Wild Strawberries,” “Beauty and the Beast,” and Max Ophuls‘ “Le plaisir” and “La ronde” (based on the play by Arthur Schnitzler, who also penned “Traumnovelle,” the source material for Kubrick’s “Eyes Wide Shut“).  
>  
> But Warren also included titles that aren’t in the Criterion Collection, like “Eraserhead,” “Citizen Kane,” “City Lights,” “The Godfather” and more surprising movies like “White Men Can’t Jump,” “Modern Romance,” and “The Jerk.” No, that’s no joke. “White Men Can’t Jump” is indeed among Stanley Kubrick’s favorite films. Perhaps it was the budding chemistry between Wesley Snipes and Woody Harrelson that won him over. Or maybe the chess playing Kubrick was also a major baller. It’s no secret that Stanley Kubrick had a wicked sense of humor, but it’s always amusing to learn about the lighter side of the late auteur.

I remember seeing him list both Audition and The Matrix on his all-time favourite list. Not that The Matrix is massively schlocky, it's well done. It's just nice that he appreciates something low-budget and shocking as well as Hollywood action.

I was pretty surprised when reading Sir Peter Jackson's biography to find that Sir John Boorman's *Excalibur* is "an absolute favourite" of his. Jackson was famous for eschewing the shorthand of 1980s fantasy, and frankly to me his films don't look, sound or feel the least bit like Excalibur. He had said that while "a couple of movies have been okay" - I'm assuming Excalibur being one of them - the fantasy genre "has never really succeeded.
